title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
authors: Ying Xie
abstract: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset. We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey. We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

infographic.key_insight: The paper mines OpenAI’s 2026 AI-generated math release to extract and catalog reusable mathematical instruments—new lemmas, constructions, inequalities, and proof mechanisms—rather than merely summarizing the claimed solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a structured way to turn large-scale AI-generated proofs into a reusable knowledge base for theorem proving, proof search, and downstream complexity or formalization research.
method: Surveyed 38 problem families across number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology, and mathematical physics.
Recorded for each entry the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents, and caveats, then grouped recurring ideas into 11 cross-cutting patterns.
Tracked formalization status and dependencies in a scoreboard while comparing source arguments against established results.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a two-stage review of 38 families and notes that no Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for the survey.
infographic.watch_item: Novelty and correctness claims are provisional: some source comparisons correct statements or counts, but they do not independently certify the proofs or establish priority.
infographic.paper_title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics

title: Boundary Control of a Modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest Beam via Reduced-Order Reinforcement Learning
authors: Leonardo R S Rodrigues
abstract: In this paper, we study the active vibration control of an elastic beam using reinforcement learning (RL). The physical system is modeled by a modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest type linear partial differential equation with simply supported boundary conditions. The dynamics are approximated by a reduced-order model (ROM) obtained through eigenvalue expansion and truncated Galerkin projection. Control is applied through boundary actuation. The resulting finite-dimensional system is formulated as a continuous-time Markov decision process and solved numerically using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. All modeling steps, from physical formulation to temporal discretization and control design, are explicitly described. A systematic comparison is performed between the controller learned via PPO and the classical linear quadratic (LQR) regulator. The analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each approach, both from a theoretical and practical point of view, with particular emphasis on energy dissipation mechanisms and actuator constraints.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that a boundary-actuated PPO reinforcement learning controller can stabilize vibrations in a reduced-order Timoshenko-Ehrenfest beam model and is benchmarked against LQR.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for vibration suppression in flexible structures where boundary actuation and model reduction must work reliably under actuator constraints.
method: Derive a modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest beam PDE with simply supported boundaries.
Build a reduced-order model using eigenfunction expansion and truncated Galerkin projection.
Formulate the finite-dimensional control problem as a continuous-time MDP and solve it with PPO; compare against LQR.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a numerical, step-by-step comparison between the PPO-learned controller and the classical LQR regulator, focusing on dissipation behavior and control constraints.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the accuracy of the reduced-order truncation, so limited modal retention may miss important beam dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Boundary Control of a Modified Timoshenko-Ehrenfest Beam via Reduced-Order Reinforcement Learning

title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
authors: Yitian Lu, Weinan Wang
abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

infographic.key_insight: Accurate tumor-growth predictions can still come from the wrong law, so symbolic discovery must be judged by mathematical validity and law recovery, not just fit quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational modeling workflows, the paper shows that coefficient refitting and candidate ranking can materially change which equations are selected, affecting downstream reliability in data-driven scientific discovery.
method: Generate sparse/noisy synthetic Gompertz tumor-growth data and compare recovered laws to the known truth.
Apply symbolic regression, admissibility screening, coefficient refitting, and LLM-based ranking to shortlist candidate equations.
Evaluate trajectory fit, forecasting, and governing-law recovery separately.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic data, dense noiseless sampling recovered the true family, while sparse noisy sampling often produced alternative forms; classical nonlinear least squares usually improved law error, but PINN refitting often worsened it.
infographic.watch_item: LLM rankings and fit-based selection can favor plausible-looking but mathematically incorrect laws, so human-checkable admissibility and independent law-recovery metrics are needed.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking

title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
authors: Futing Wang, Chenxi Li, Jianhao Yan, Yun Luo, Zhi Wang, Yizhuo Li
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.

infographic.key_insight: TPPO replaces a standard PPO critic with a cumulative, prefix-tracking value model that better follows token-level value evolution under sparse terminal rewards.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves reasoning-policy training stability and credit assignment for LLMs, yielding stronger math reasoning and better out-of-distribution generalization across model sizes and tasks.
method: Model successive prefix values with a Bayesian decomposition in log-odds space
Predict position-wise scalar outputs and sum them into value logits
Train the reconstructed values using terminal-outcome supervision
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports aggregate math reasoning gains of +7.0 on Qwen3-4B-Base and +8.4 on Qwen3-8B-Base, with improvements also on Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B, countdown, and scientific coding tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Because the method relies on reconstructed cumulative value logits and terminal supervision, it may be sensitive to value calibration and implementation details in sparse-reward settings.
infographic.paper_title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning

title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Haolin Tian, Yikang Li, Tonghan Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.

infographic.key_insight: GrowRL turns RL updates into explicit, reusable Transformer pathways by freezing the backbone and training only newly added attention and feed-forward branches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes RL adaptation more parameter-efficient and transferable, so one expensive reasoning training run can be reused across compatible LLMs.
method: Freeze the pretrained backbone and add a causal-attention branch plus a feed-forward branch at each Transformer layer.
Zero-initialize output projections so the model initially matches the pretrained policy, then update only the added pathways with RL.
Keep the learned pathways explicit for transfer to target models, with support for sequential transfer of additional pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five backbones, the method reports competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with few trainable parameters, and target-side transfer is already close after 10 updates versus 100.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer requires structural compatibility between source and target models, and the added branching may complicate implementation and deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
authors: Mattie Ji, Indradyumna Roy, Vikas Garg
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows how to generate graphs that match a target persistence diagram exactly, rather than only approximately, by using either iterative local rules or a complete global constraint-satisfaction formulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables topology-controlled graph generation for computational science workflows where exact structural guarantees matter, such as design, synthesis, and benchmarking.
method: Local method: iteratively construct degree-based PD-equivalent graphs and prove every output matches the target PD.
Local method: show reachability of all degree-based PD-equivalent graphs, but note a trade-off with diversity and infeasible states.

Global method: encode exact topological compliance as a complete constraint program solvable by modern solvers; works for vertex-based permutation-equivariant filtrations and is minimal under degree filtration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on four standard graph-generation benchmarks show that both methods realize the target persistence diagram exactly.
infographic.watch_item: The local approach can reduce sample diversity and may encounter infeasible states, while the global solver-based approach may depend on constraint-programming scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs

title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
authors: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

infographic.key_insight: LeanPRM uses Lean to automatically generate step-level correctness labels for natural-language proofs, avoiding costly human annotation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a scalable training pipeline for proof verifiers that can improve step checking and proof selection across model sizes.
method: Generate a natural-language proof and a paired formal Lean proof with no Lean feedback.
Use Lean to label each proof step, then filter out syntax-only failures so negatives reflect mathematical errors.
Train a process verifier on the resulting step-labeled dataset.
infographic.evidence_signal: LeanPRM includes 10,634 proofs and 152K labeled steps; a Qwen3-4B verifier improved exact step-label accuracy on LeanPRM-Bench from 48.2 to 74.7, outperforming a PRM800K-trained baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Quality depends on the alignment between natural-language and formal Lean proofs, so formalization mismatches or noisy translations could still bias labels.
infographic.paper_title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification

title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus
authors: Neil Walton
abstract: We develop a rate-transfer method that converts finite-time Lyapunov estimates for an associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) into finite-time convergence bounds for stochastic gradient algorithms. Under generic moment and smoothness conditions, the convergence analysis of the stochastic gradient method reduces to a calculus argument verifying a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE. The method recovers established rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and provides a way to establish convergence rates for new optimization algorithms through calculus arguments applied to their associated SDEs.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a rate-transfer method that turns finite-time Lyapunov bounds for an associated SDE into finite-time convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient algorithms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives optimization practitioners a calculus-based way to derive and verify convergence rates for SGD-like methods, including new algorithm variants, without redoing the full stochastic analysis.
method: Build an SDE that corresponds to the stochastic gradient algorithm.
Prove a Lyapunov generator inequality for the SDE using calculus.
Transfer the resulting finite-time SDE rate bound back to the discrete algorithm.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the method recovers established convergence rates for classical stochastic gradient methods and extends to new algorithms through SDE-based calculus arguments.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on suitable moment and smoothness conditions plus a valid SDE approximation, so rate guarantees may be harder to apply when assumptions are violated.
infographic.paper_title: A Rate Transfer Method: Convergence Rates in Stochastic Gradient Descent via Stochastic Calculus

title: Towards learning-enhanced solvers for multi-parametric optimization
authors: Dieter Teichrib, Fabian König, Moritz Schulze Darup
abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have been employed in various ways to accelerate the solution of multi-parametric optimization problems (OPs), which prominently arise in model predictive control (MPC). Early approaches focused on approximating the parametric solution (e.g., the optimal control law) directly by NNs. More recently, learning-based techniques have been used to emulate or enhance solver iterations. For the direct approximation of the parametric solution, it has been demonstrated that exploiting structural properties of the underlying OP facilitates the design of suitable NN architectures. In this paper, we show that structural analysis can also be leveraged to systematically integrate learning into classical optimization algorithms, thereby enhancing their performance. We formalize our concept for the case of multi-parametric quadratic programs (mpQPs), which frequently arise in linear-quadratic MPC, as a representative application. More precisely, we demonstrate that tailored NNs enable a parameter-dependent fine-tuning of the step sizes in a standard dual projected gradient scheme. The design of the NNs is guided by the observation that optimal step sizes, which permit obtaining the exact optimal solution in finitely many iterations, are piecewise constant functions over the parameter space (e.g., the state space in MPC). We establish key theoretical properties of the proposed approach and illustrate its effectiveness in a numerical case study.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that learning can improve classical optimization solvers by using neural networks to adapt solver step sizes in a parameter-dependent way.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for MPC and other real-time control applications because it can reduce iterations while preserving the structure of exact optimization methods.
method: Analyze the structure of multi-parametric quadratic programs to identify how optimal solver settings vary across the parameter space.
Use tailored neural networks to predict piecewise-constant step sizes for a dual projected gradient method.
Integrate the learned step-size tuning into a standard solver rather than replacing the solver itself.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical properties of the method and a numerical case study demonstrating its effectiveness on mpQPs.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurately learning piecewise-constant step-size regions, so performance may degrade if the parameter-space partition is poorly captured.
infographic.paper_title: Towards learning-enhanced solvers for multi-parametric optimization

title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
authors: Maor Ben Shahar, Jonathan Morag, Dirk Englund, Kfir Sulimany
abstract: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

infographic.key_insight: The paper formalizes an end-to-end, composable security proof for entanglement-based BB84 in Lean, removing hidden assumptions and enabling machine-checked quantum cryptography proofs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This creates a reproducible standard for verifying quantum security arguments and shows that theorem provers plus LLM autoformalization can accelerate both proof construction and protocol optimization.
method: Formalized the BB84 security theorem in Lean using only standard axioms
Proved composable security against coherent attacks via the postselection technique
Used an LLM-based autoformalization pipeline to translate and refine the proof
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a complete Lean formalization of composable security for entanglement-based qubit BB84 with finite block-size accounting and a subsequent reduction in the finite-size key-rate penalty.
infographic.watch_item: The result depends on the fidelity of the Lean formalization and the modeling assumptions chosen for local operations, classical communication, and the postselection-based security framework.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean

title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making
authors: Jing Liu, Yongxing Qi, Ping Yao, Ting Wu
abstract: What binds large language models on auditable, hypothesis-driven decision tasks, where every candidate can be checked against the evidence? On the public TCMEval-SDT benchmark for Traditional Chinese Medicine syndrome differentiation (200 cases), the binding constraint is output discipline and reasoning structure, not model capability alone: two years of model scaling move zero-shot scores by only -0.03 to +0.08, while output-discipline failures (non-terminating reasoning, format non-compliance, large run-to-run spread) persist even in frontier models. We test this with a model-agnostic agent framework formalizing decision making as a five-stage closed loop, enforced by a candidate x evidence matrix falsification protocol: every candidate is judged against every evidence item, at least half of the candidates must be falsified before a conclusion is licensed, and survivors are emitted in a machine-verifiable single-line format. Across five base models, the effect is sign-conditional on zero-shot output discipline: it rescues models whose discipline fails (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: +0.267/+0.271, entirely termination rescue), reduces a high-variance model's run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007 (Kimi K3), and significantly costs already-disciplined models (-0.087 to -0.120 on budget-matched Qwen3-4B/32B). Ablations attribute the cost to the candidate-bounded format layer and show the effect is independent of injected knowledge content (protocol-knowledge decoupling). The protocol also transfers to misinformation-robust mathematical reasoning, detecting injected false premises at 89.8% recall with a 6.8% false-positive rate (MCC 0.54; a flag-everything baseline scores 0) and restoring accuracy to the no-misinformation ceiling. Where zero-shot output discipline is weak, the reasoning protocol sets the floor; base-model capability always sets the ceiling.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that for auditable hypothesis-driven decisions, output discipline and structured reasoning matter more than raw model scale, and a falsification-guided protocol can expose and control that weakness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A model-agnostic closed-loop protocol can make LLM decision pipelines more reliable and machine-checkable, especially when outputs must be auditable and evidence-linked.
method: Formalize decision making as a five-stage closed loop.
Use a candidate × evidence matrix to falsify every candidate against every evidence item.
Require at least half of candidates to be rejected before a conclusion is emitted in a single-line verifiable format.
infographic.evidence_signal: On TCMEval-SDT (200 cases), the protocol improved weak-discipline models such as DeepSeek-V4-Flash by about +0.27, cut Kimi K3 run-to-run standard deviation from 0.218 to 0.007, and showed mixed or negative effects on already disciplined models.
infographic.watch_item: The protocol can hurt models that already have strong output discipline, so deployment should be gated by benchmarked discipline/variance rather than assumed universally beneficial.
infographic.paper_title: Output Discipline Sets the Floor: A Falsification-Guided, Model-Agnostic Agent Protocol for Auditable Hypothesis-Driven Decision Making

title: QEDIA: Quantum Program Verification in Lean
authors: Yuanjie, Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Junyi Liu, Jinzheng Li, Yidi Qi
abstract: Practical quantum programs interleave quantum and classical computation: classical data shape the quantum operations that are performed, and measurement outcomes shape the classical computation that follows. Formal verification of such programs in a proof assistant requires mechanizing a program logic that handles this interplay consistently at every level, from the mathematics of quantum mechanics, through program syntax and semantics, to specifications and proof rules. Such mechanizations, along with the program proofs built on them, typically require substantial manual effort. We present QEDIA, a framework for verifying quantum programs with classical variables in Lean 4. At its foundation is an open library that formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ across all these levels and proves the logic sound for both partial and total correctness. We construct the library and the program proofs, under human supervision, using an LLM-based prover agent, whose general-purpose core we extend for quantum program verification. We illustrate QEDIA with verified programs including the quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.

infographic.key_insight: QEDIA shows that quantum programs mixing classical and quantum control can be formally verified in Lean 4 by mechanizing both the quantum Hoare logic and its soundness end-to-end.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical path toward trustworthy quantum software by enabling machine-checked proofs for real quantum algorithms with classical variables and measurement-driven control flow.
method: Formalize quantum mechanics, program syntax/semantics, specifications, and proof rules in Lean 4.
Implement the open QHL+ library and prove soundness for both partial and total correctness.
Use an LLM-based prover agent, under human supervision, to build the library and verify example programs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports verified case studies including quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.
infographic.watch_item: The workflow still relies on human supervision and an extended prover agent, so scalability and robustness on larger quantum developments remain a concern.
infographic.paper_title: QEDIA: Quantum Program Verification in Lean

title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
authors: Zikun Zhang, Jiayuan Sheng, David D. Yao, Wenpin Tang
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

infographic.key_insight: JustOPD adapts on-policy distillation to transfer reasoning ability from a strong autoregressive teacher to a diffusion language model by using autoregressive rollouts during training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical route to improve DLM mathematical reasoning without sacrificing their flexible generation-order inference behavior.
method: Train the DLM student on sequences sampled from its own policy during distillation.
Use autoregressive rollouts to align the student’s training trajectory with the teacher’s left-to-right decoding.
Support multiple divergence objectives while distilling from Qwen3-14B to Dream-7B.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent mathematical reasoning gains over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices in experiments with Qwen3-14B as teacher and Dream-7B as student.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on successful alignment between AR teacher rollouts and the DLM training process, which may add implementation complexity and still leave teacher-student mismatch issues.
infographic.paper_title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models

title: A Lean formalisation of the disproof of Ramaekers's conjecture
authors: Jeremy Tan
abstract: We describe Redhill, a Lean formalisation of the major results in Hölzl, Kleine and Stephan's "Improved Lower Bounds for Strong $n$-Conjectures" (arXiv:2409.13439). Design decisions regarding types and data structures are justified as enabling canonical versions of the paper's claims, and from there the most direct proofs of said claims. The formalisation process also uncovered many errors, omissions and optimisation opportunities in the informal proof, all of which are addressed in the final library. Although Redhill is meant to stand alone, a few lemmas were upstreamed to the primary Lean mathematics library mathlib. We discuss the tension between upstreaming and leaving lemmas in separate libraries. Unlike many other contemporary formalisation projects, Redhill was completed without any assistance from large language models (LLMs). We compare our work with LLM-assisted projects, in particular an extension of arXiv:2409.13439 to $n=4$, aiming to establish design and style guidelines that define good Lean formalisations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents Redhill, a Lean formalization of the disproof of Ramaekers's conjecture, emphasizing canonical definitions and direct proofs to make the informal argument machine-checkable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It highlights how careful choices of types, data structures, and library boundaries can improve proof robustness, reuse, and maintainability in formal verification projects.
method: Formalized the main results from a recent proof paper in Lean
Chose canonical representations to simplify statements and proofs
Upstreamed some lemmas to mathlib while keeping the rest in a standalone library
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the formalization exposed multiple errors, omissions, and optimization opportunities in the informal proof, all of which were resolved in the final library.
infographic.watch_item: A key implementation concern is the tension between upstreaming lemmas to a shared library and keeping them in a separate project, which can affect portability and reuse.
infographic.paper_title: A Lean formalisation of the disproof of Ramaekers's conjecture

title: Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Policy Reinforcement Learning for Derivative-Free Model-Based Control
authors: K. Rabiei, Z. Rui, X. Lu, W. Hao
abstract: Finite-horizon optimal control becomes difficult when a dynamical model can be simulated reliably, but its derivatives are unavailable, discontinuous, or unreliable. Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Policy Optimization (HPDPO) is introduced as a derivative-free, model-based reinforcement learning framework for this setting. The control is represented as a time-indexed finite-horizon policy. Candidate actions are evaluated by deterministic suffix rollouts of the supplied transition model, while a regularized Hamiltonian dual formulation supplies structured future-cost information through block-coordinate multiplier updates. No differentiation of the state dynamics or learned critic is required. The method is validated on nonsmooth problems with exact solutions, an analytical and learned ReLU biomarker cascade, an amyloid Neural ODE trained from longitudinal ADNI data, and three multidimensional-control problems with up to five simultaneous controls. Across these examples, HPDPO closely reproduces exact or reference objective values, trajectories, and control structures. The results show that forward simulation and Hamiltonian dual structure can be combined to solve deterministic finite-horizon control problems involving nonsmooth, learned, or black-box dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: HPDPO solves finite-horizon control without model derivatives by combining forward rollouts with a Hamiltonian primal-dual update to estimate future cost structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is useful for control systems with reliable simulators but nonsmooth, learned, or black-box dynamics where gradients are unavailable or unstable.
method: Represent control as a finite-horizon time-indexed policy.
Evaluate candidate actions using deterministic suffix rollouts of the transition model.
Use a regularized Hamiltonian dual formulation with block-coordinate multiplier updates instead of differentiating dynamics or a critic.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is validated on exact/nonsmooth benchmarks, a biomarker cascade, an amyloid Neural ODE from ADNI data, and three multidimensional control problems, where it closely matches reference objectives, trajectories, and controls.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on having a reliable forward simulator and may be sensitive to rollout horizon, multiplier regularization, and block-update tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Policy Reinforcement Learning for Derivative-Free Model-Based Control

title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models
authors: Zhaohui Zheng, Chenhang He, Jinrui Zhang, Ming-Ming Cheng, Lei Zhang
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have attracted increasing research attention due to their bidirectional attention and arbitrary order decoding. However, there are two issues in dLLMs inference: the decoding difficulty is dominated by the tokens on the right side of the block, and the block-wise decoding inherently suffers from boundary contextual discontinuity. To tackle these limitations, we propose HaloBlock, a difficulty-aware adaptive halo mechanism for dLLM inference. We first leverage bidirectional cumulative entropy to characterize block decoding difficulty. Then, based on the bidirectional decoding difficulty, we adaptively allocate bidirectional halo regions on both sides of each block to mitigate boundary contextual discontinuity. The difficulty-aware design of HaloBlock smooths cross-block context propagation and lowers decoding difficulty for hard tokens, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence. Evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, HaloBlock demonstrates consistent accuracy improvements and higher inference efficiency. Source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/HaloBlock.

infographic.key_insight: HaloBlock improves diffusion LLM decoding by measuring block difficulty and adding adaptive bidirectional halo context to reduce boundary discontinuity and lower hard-token decoding cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical inference-time strategy to make dLLMs faster and more accurate on reasoning and code tasks without changing the base model architecture.
method: Compute bidirectional cumulative entropy to estimate decoding difficulty for each block.
Allocate adaptive halo regions on both left and right sides of blocks based on difficulty.
Use the added cross-block context to smooth boundary effects and improve convergence/quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, Dream-7B-Instruct, and LLaDA-1.5 across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, showing consistent accuracy gains and higher inference efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: Adaptive halo sizing may increase implementation complexity and inference overhead if block difficulty estimates are noisy or poorly calibrated.
infographic.paper_title: HaloBlock: Faster and Better Decoding for Diffusion Large Language Models

title: Efficient Shallow Ritz Method: 1D Semi-Linear Diffusion-Reaction and Allen-Cahn Equations
authors: Zhiqiang Cai, César Herrera
abstract: An efficient shallow Ritz method was developed in [8, 9] for one-dimensional linear diffusion and diffusion-reaction problems. In this paper, the method is extended to a nonlinear diffusion-reaction equation with a cubic reaction term: (1) a basic error estimate of the shallow Ritz discretization is established and (2) a reduced block Newton (rBN) method for solving the resulting non-convex optimization problem is developed. Again, the computational cost of the rBN method is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ for one-dimensional problems, where $n$ is the number of neurons. Combining a convex splitting scheme for time discretization with the efficient shallow Ritz method, we develop a time-stepping neural network method for solving the Allen-Cahn equation. The unconditional energy stability of the time discretization and an error estimate in the $L^2$ norm are established. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the neural network approach yields accurate solutions for singularly perturbed nonlinear diffusion-reaction equations and the Allen-Cahn equation. The method effectively resolves interior and boundary layers without oscillations and significantly outperforms the finite element method on fixed uniform meshes.

infographic.key_insight: A shallow neural Ritz method can efficiently solve 1D nonlinear diffusion-reaction and Allen-Cahn equations with linear-in-neuron computational cost while preserving accuracy and stability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a scalable physics-informed alternative to finite elements for stiff nonlinear PDEs, especially when boundary/interior layers must be resolved on fixed meshes.
method: Extend shallow Ritz to cubic nonlinear diffusion-reaction.
Use a reduced block Newton solver with O(n) cost in 1D.
Combine convex splitting time stepping with the neural solver for Allen-Cahn.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports error estimates, unconditional energy stability, and numerical experiments showing accurate layer resolution and better performance than finite elements on uniform meshes.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is tailored to 1D settings and relies on solving a non-convex optimization problem, so robustness may depend on initialization and extension to higher dimensions.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Shallow Ritz Method: 1D Semi-Linear Diffusion-Reaction and Allen-Cahn Equations

title: Optimal Feature-Based Newsvendor Policies under Censored Demand
authors: Joost van der Haar, Ilias Willems, Joachim Arts, Ingrid Van Keilegom
abstract: We investigate a newsvendor problem where a decision-maker observes a $z$-dimensional vector of covariates, and wants to learn how much stock to order given a sample of size $n$ of censored demand data to minimize costs. Demand is censored when insufficient stock is available to meet it, and past stocking quantities are known. We propose a new model-agnostic loss function approach to estimate optimal order quantities using observational data, and characterize the optimal newsvendor policy as the policy that minimizes our proposed loss function. Our method requires only a single estimation step, can be scaled to datasets with hundreds of thousands of data points, and does not suffer from the same instabilities as inverse censoring probability weighting methods. We describe how this loss function can be implemented in linear empirical risk minimization, kernel weights optimization and deep neural network algorithms, and provide excess risk generalization bounds for their out-of-sample performance. Moreover, we show through numerical experiments that our method quickly converges to the optimal policy on synthetic data, and leads to improved performance on real world retail data.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that optimal stock orders under censored demand can be learned directly from covariates by minimizing a new model-agnostic loss function, avoiding explicit demand reconstruction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives practitioners a scalable way to build data-driven inventory policies from real retail logs, with implementations compatible with linear models, kernel methods, and deep networks.
method: Defines a custom loss whose minimizer matches the optimal newsvendor policy under censored observations.
Uses a single estimation step on observational data with known past stocking quantities.
Provides excess-risk generalization bounds for linear, kernel, and neural network implementations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fast convergence on synthetic data and improved performance on real-world retail data, with scalability to hundreds of thousands of samples.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of observed covariates and censored-demand data, and practical results may vary if the censoring mechanism or past-order information is noisy.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal Feature-Based Newsvendor Policies under Censored Demand

title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR
authors: Daijiao Liu, Huiyi Wang, Lina Yao, Dong Gong
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

infographic.key_insight: EDEN boosts RLVR exploration by perturbing the input embedding at rollout time, creating more diverse trajectories without changing the model architecture or inference pipeline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a lightweight, training-time-only way to improve mathematical reasoning coverage and strengthen group-relative learning signals under the same rollout budget.
method: Adds a single perturbed embedding position to some prompts as an anchored source of directional noise.
Uses Gaussian noise plus a shared anchor to keep perturbations diverse yet group-consistent.
Mixes selected perturbed rollouts into GRPO with downweighted advantages; decoding and test-time inference stay unchanged.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple model scales and math-reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperformed GRPO and other exploration controls, with the biggest gains in sampled solution coverage and more groups receiving non-zero learning signals.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on careful tuning of noise level, anchor design, and the fraction of perturbed rollouts to avoid destabilizing training or weakening useful advantage signals.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR

title: VeriPIE: Checkable Query Plans and Evidence-Guided Selection for Text-to-SQL
authors: Piyush Jha, Cruise Song, Zhengyu Li, Yatharth Sejpal
abstract: Financial Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and model risk management (MRM) emphasize independent validation, transparency, and effective challenge of AI-generated computations. Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into Structured Query Language (SQL), but queries that agree on one database can still express different computations. We present VeriPIE, a neurosymbolic framework combining language-model generation with symbolic checks. It ensembles direct SQL generation with QuerySketch, a structured plan language checked by a backend implemented in Lean, a theorem prover and programming language. Plan diagnostics guide repair before SQL generation, while execution agreement and bounded searches for distinguishing databases inform candidate selection. These checks expose malformed plans and hidden disagreement without proving agreement with the user's intent. In single-run experiments on the complete Spider development set, VeriPIE achieves 72.05% test-suite accuracy (745/1,034), compared with DeepEye's 65.67% (679/1,034). Its two-query shortlist covers 78.43% (811 questions), compared with 74.66% for DIN-SQL (772) and 69.05% for DeepEye (714). On BIRD, VeriPIE reaches 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage. The central benefit is reviewable evidence about the generated computation: explicit plan checks, repair diagnostics, and concrete disagreements that support safer financial analysis.

infographic.key_insight: VeriPIE combines text-to-SQL generation with theorem-prover-checked query plans and evidence-based candidate selection to make generated computations more reviewable and trustworthy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is relevant for high-stakes analytics because it adds symbolic validation, repair diagnostics, and disagreement evidence before a SQL query is trusted or executed.
method: Generate both direct SQL and a structured QuerySketch plan.
Check plans with a Lean-based symbolic backend and use diagnostics to repair malformed plans.
Use execution agreement and bounded searches for distinguishing databases to rank candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Spider development, VeriPIE reports 72.05% test-suite accuracy and 78.43% two-query shortlist coverage; on BIRD it reaches 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage.
infographic.watch_item: The system provides evidence about the generated computation, but it does not prove the query matches the user’s intent, so human review is still needed.
infographic.paper_title: VeriPIE: Checkable Query Plans and Evidence-Guided Selection for Text-to-SQL
